title: Target Wake Time & Battery Life
summary: Scheduled wake-ups that let badges and sensors sleep, plus protected time slots for urgent traffic.

opener.promise: Devices sleep between agreed wake-ups, so batteries can last longer
opener.problem: Badges and tags drain their batteries listening for messages that rarely come.

wifi7Adds: Target Wake Time was first defined in 802.11ah {{twt-origin}} and came to mainstream Wi-Fi with Wi-Fi 6 {{twt-wifi6}}; Wi-Fi 7 adds optional Restricted TWT, which protects time slots for latency-sensitive traffic {{rtwt-be}} {{rtwt-optional}}.

beats.heading: Always listening, flat by mid-shift

caption.headline: Always listening, flat by mid-shift
caption.takeaway: Radios that never sleep drain batteries, leaving clinicians or equipment unreachable until recharged.

beats.body:
[[voice-badge|Voice badges]], [[rtls|location tags]] and wearable [[patient-monitor|patient monitors]] are small, battery-powered devices. Without a schedule, their radios stay ready to listen in case the [[access-point|access point]] has something for them, and listening costs power even when nothing arrives.

The result is batteries swapped or recharged mid-shift, and devices that go quiet when a battery runs out.
beats.bottomLine: Battery swaps cost staff time and can leave clinicians or equipment unreachable until a device is recharged.
beats.sceneDescription: One ward over one shift. A voice badge, a location tag and a patient monitor stand under the access point, each with a large battery above it and its radio glowing to show it is always listening. As the shift bar along the front fills, every battery drains from green through amber to red, and the badge goes flat before the shift ends. Battery levels are labelled illustrative.

callout.title: Why batteries run out
points: Radios stay awake listening, even when nothing arrives
Listening drains the battery all shift long
A flat badge or tag means an unreachable clinician or lost equipment

beats.heading: Agree when to wake, sleep in between

caption.headline: Agree when to wake, sleep in between
caption.takeaway: With [[twt|Target Wake Time]], devices sleep between agreed wake-ups{{twt-what}}, so batteries can last longer.

beats.body: With [[twt|Target Wake Time]], each device and its access point agree on when the device will wake up to exchange data, so it can sleep in between {{twt-what}}. TWT was first defined in IEEE 802.11ah {{twt-origin}} and became a core feature of Wi-Fi 6 {{twt-wifi6}}.
beats.bottomLine: Battery-powered clinical devices spend more time asleep, so they can last longer between charges.
beats.sceneDescription: The same shift again, now with Target Wake Time. Marks on the shift bar show the agreed wake-ups. Each device stays dark and asleep, glowing and linking to the access point only briefly at its own wake-up times. The batteries drain more slowly and have more charge left at the end of the shift. Battery levels are illustrative.

questions.q: How much longer will batteries last?
questions.a: It depends on the device and how often it must wake, so no single figure applies. Ask vendors for battery data with TWT enabled, and test with your own traffic.

questions.q: Isn’t TWT already part of Wi-Fi 6?
questions.a: Yes. TWT came to mainstream Wi-Fi with Wi-Fi 6{{twt-wifi6}}, after first appearing in 802.11ah{{twt-origin}}. Wi-Fi 7 adds Restricted TWT, which protects the medium during service periods{{rtwt-be}}.

callout.title: What Target Wake Time changes
points: Each device and the access point agree when it will wake{{twt-what}}
Between wake-ups the radio sleeps and saves battery
The access point holds messages until the next wake-up

beats.heading: Schedules for one device or a whole group

caption.headline: Schedules for one device or a whole group
caption.takeaway: Access points can coordinate groups of tags and badges with shared wake schedules{{twt-types-ax}}.
caption.technical: Individual and broadcast TWT{{twt-types-ax}}; each [[service-period|service period]] is set by wake time, interval and duration.

beats.body: A device can negotiate its own schedule, or join a schedule the access point announces for a group of devices {{twt-types-ax}}. Between its wake windows, the device can switch its radio off; the access point holds traffic for it until the next [[service-period|service period]] {{twt-what}}.
beats.bottomLine: Access points can coordinate many low-power devices at once, which matters on floors with large numbers of tags and badges.
beats.deepDive: 802.11ax supports individual TWT agreements negotiated per station and broadcast TWT schedules advertised by the AP for groups of stations {{twt-types-ax}}. The agreed parameters include the target wake time, the wake interval and the minimum wake duration, which together define each service period {{twt-what}}.
beats.sceneDescription: The access point announces one wake-up time for the whole group. At each mark on the shift bar, all three devices wake together, exchange data and go back to sleep, and the access point glows as it serves them in one go. Batteries stay high.

callout.title: One schedule, many devices
points: A device can agree its own wake-up times{{twt-types-ax}}
Or join one schedule the access point shares with a group
Large groups of tags stay organised and save battery

beats.heading: Protected time for urgent traffic

caption.headline: Protected time for urgent traffic
caption.takeaway: Optional [[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]] reserves protected slots for voice and alarms{{rtwt-be}}{{rtwt-optional}}.
caption.technical: Supporting stations end their transmissions before each restricted service period begins{{rtwt-protect}}.

beats.body:
TWT saves power, but it does not stop a busy laptop from occupying the air just when a voice packet is due. Wi-Fi 7 adds [[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]], which reserves protected service periods for latency-sensitive traffic {{rtwt-be}}. It is optional: only access points and devices that support it take part {{rtwt-optional}}.

Devices that support it are expected to finish transmitting before a protected period begins {{rtwt-protect}}. Devices that do not, and interference from outside the network, are not held back.
beats.bottomLine: Where access points and devices support it, voice and alarm traffic can get more predictable time on the air; check support model by model.
beats.deepDive: Restricted TWT (r-TWT) builds on broadcast TWT: the AP advertises restricted service periods for specified traffic identifiers, and supporting stations end their transmission opportunities before each period starts {{rtwt-protect}}. Earlier generations without TWT keep devices awake {{twt-what}}; Wi-Fi 6 TWT schedules wake-ups but does not protect the medium during them {{twt-types-ax}}.
beats.sceneDescription: A laptop that supports Restricted TWT joins the ward, downloading over a thick link to the access point. Whenever the badge’s protected slot comes round, the laptop is marked paused, its link goes quiet, and the badge’s call goes through before the laptop resumes. A note shows that the earlier generation had no protected time slots. The badge still sleeps between wake-ups.

questions.q: Will Restricted TWT slow down other users?
questions.a: Slightly, during the protected slots: supporting devices pause before each one{{rtwt-protect}}. The slots are reserved only for traffic that needs them, such as voice and telemetry.

questions.q: Is Restricted TWT widely supported today?
questions.a: Do not assume it. It is optional in 802.11be{{rtwt-optional}}, so confirm support for each access point, client model and firmware version before relying on it.

callout.title: What Wi-Fi 7 adds
points: Optional [[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]] reserves protected slots for urgent traffic{{rtwt-optional}}
Supporting devices pause before each slot begins{{rtwt-protect}}
Check support in each access point, device and firmware

beats.heading: Longer battery life and dependable calls

caption.headline: Longer battery life, more predictable calls
caption.takeaway: Gains need support in each device, so ask vendors about TWT and Restricted TWT.

beats.body:
For care teams, TWT can mean fewer battery changes and devices that stay reachable through a shift, while Restricted TWT, where supported, can make voice and [[telemetry|telemetry]] timing more predictable {{rtwt-optional}}.

The gains depend on support in each device and in the access points, so include TWT and Restricted TWT in device evaluations and ask for measured battery data.
beats.bottomLine: Ask device vendors about TWT and Restricted TWT support; the access points enable them, but battery and [[latency|latency]] gains only appear on devices that use them.
beats.sceneDescription: The whole shift with both features on: the devices sleep between wake-ups, the laptop pauses for protected slots, and the batteries have more charge left at the end of the shift than without a schedule. Battery levels are illustrative.

callout.title: What to ask vendors
points: Does the device support Target Wake Time?
Battery data with TWT on, tested with our own traffic
Restricted TWT support for voice badges and monitors

lineage.lead: First defined in IEEE 802.11ah; mainstream with Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax).
